title: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Classification of Elements — 2024
subject: chemistry
topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Chemistry — Classification of Elements — 2024
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What is the modern periodic law? Explain how it improved on Mendeleev's periodic law.
questions.solution:
**Modern periodic law:** properties of elements are periodic functions of their **atomic numbers**.

It fixed Mendeleev (atomic-mass) defects: (1) anomalous pairs (Ar/K, Co/Ni) fall in correct order; (2) no unexplained gaps remain — all 118 elements placed; (3) noble gases get a natural group without disturbing the table.
questions.knowledgeNote: Moseley (1913) and X-ray spectra moved the table from mass to atomic number.

questions.question: What are s-, p-, d-, and f-blocks? Give one element belonging to each.
questions.solution:
Blocks named by the subshell receiving the last electron: **s-block** — Na; **p-block** — Cl; **d-block** (transition metals) — Fe; **f-block** (inner transition) — U.

s + p = representative elements; d = transition; f = lanthanides/actinides.
questions.knowledgeNote: Helium (1s²) sits with the p-block noble gases by behaviour, not by configuration — the famous exception.

questions.question: Define ionisation energy. Explain why nitrogen has a higher first ionisation energy than oxygen.
questions.solution:
**Ionisation energy** is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom.

N (1s² 2s² 2p³) has a **half-filled p subshell** — extra stable. Removing its electron breaks that stability, costing more energy than removing one from O (2p⁴), where repulsion between paired electrons actually helps ejection.
questions.knowledgeNote: Half-filled/full subshells (N, P, Be, Mg, noble gases) always spike above the trend — the standard 'anomaly' question.

questions.question: Define electronegativity. How does it vary across a period and down a group? Which element is the most electronegative?
questions.solution:
**Electronegativity** is an atom's pull on shared bond electrons.

It **increases left→right** (rising nuclear charge) and **decreases top→bottom** (larger, shielded atoms). **Fluorine (4.0)** is the maximum.
questions.knowledgeNote: Noble gases have no EN values (no bonds to pull in) — a tidy one-mark follow-up.

questions.question: How does atomic radius vary across a period and down a group? Explain the trend in each case.
questions.solution:
**Across a period it shrinks:** added protons pull the same shell tighter.

**Down a group it grows:** each new principal shell outweighs the extra nuclear charge.
questions.knowledgeNote: Cations < parent atom < anions — size order within one element's ions.

questions.question: What is diagonal relationship? Give one example with cause.
questions.solution:
Diagonally adjacent elements (e.g. **Li and Mg**) resemble each other more than their own group members.

Cause: similar charge density (charge/radius) — moving right shrinks size while moving down grows it, roughly cancelling along the diagonal. Both form nitrides, sparingly soluble carbonates, and similar organometallics.
questions.knowledgeNote: Li–Mg, Be–Al, B–Si are the three classic diagonal pairs.
